---
title: "Binary outcomes"
subtitle: "Risk ratio, odds ratio and risk difference from event counts"
---

Use this module when each study reports how many events occurred in each group
and the size of each group. That covers yes or no outcomes: mortality,
recurrence, response to treatment.

If your effect already comes calculated from the paper, the right module is
[pre-calculated effects](precalculated.qmd), not this one.

This page covers what belongs to this module. The screens and the buttons are in
[the three-step flow](flow.qmd).

## Step 1, the data

Five required columns, with these exact names:

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `study` | the study label, for example "Silva 2019" |
| `event.e` | events in the experimental group |
| `n.e` | size of the experimental group |
| `event.c` | events in the control group |
| `n.c` | size of the control group |

Any extra column is optional and becomes available later, for subgroup analysis
and meta-regression. The example dataset carries `Region`, `Design`,
`RiskOfBias`, `MeanAge` and `FollowUpMonths`.

## Step 2, the parameters

### Summary measure (sm)

Default `RR`. It decides what gets pooled:

* `RR`, risk ratio. The easiest to communicate and the most used in clinical
  trials. Recommended as a starting point.
* `OR`, odds ratio. Needed if you will compare against literature that uses OR,
  or if you intend to use the Peto or GLMM methods, which only work with `OR`.
  Remember that the OR drifts away from the RR when the event is common.
* `RD`, risk difference, on the absolute scale. Useful for communicating
  clinical impact ("7 fewer events per 100 patients"), but usually more
  heterogeneous across studies than the relative measures.

### Method

Default `inverse`. It is the pooling method, and it exists only in this module
and in single proportions:

* `inverse`, inverse variance. The app default, and it serves well when studies
  are of reasonable size and events are not rare.
* `MH`, Mantel-Haenszel. Behaves better than inverse variance when there are few
  events or small studies. It is the Cochrane default for binary data.
  Recommended if your outcome is uncommon.
* `Peto`. Suits very rare events with groups of similar size. Only works with
  `sm = OR`.
* `GLMM`, generalized linear mixed model. Avoids the continuity corrections the
  other methods apply to zero cells. Slower. Only works with `sm = OR`, and the
  forest plot comes out without the Weight column, because a GLMM fit produces
  no per-study weight.

::: {.callout-important}
## Peto and GLMM require OR
If you leave `sm = RR` or `sm = RD` and pick `Peto` or `GLMM`, the analysis
stops with an error message. Switch `sm` to `OR` first, or set the method back
to `inverse` or `MH`.
:::

### The other fields

**Outcome name**, the outcome direction and the group names work as described in
[Outcome settings](flow.qmd#outcome-settings).

**Analysis model**, **Tau method**, **Random CI method** and **Prediction
method** work and are recommended as in
[Statistical settings (advanced)](flow.qmd#statistical-settings-advanced). In
this module the **Prediction interval** is off by default.

## Step 3, export and results

This module carries the full set of cards: forest plot, leave-one-out, funnel
plot, small-study effects with Egger's test, subgroup analysis, meta-regression
and the two summary tables as XLSX. All of them are described in
[step 3 of the flow](flow.qmd).
